MercadoLibre is heading into its November 4 third quarter report after heavy spending on Brazilian logistics and credit expansion, with management reiterating that Brazil's credit trends remain stable despite recent political shifts.

The firm has intentionally accepted lower operating margins through fee cuts and free shipping in Brazil. Citi's upgrade highlights how these reinvestment choices and credit quality signals are reshaping external expectations for the business.

We will now explore how MercadoLibre's investment narrative could be influenced by Brazil focused reinvestment and the upcoming earnings release.

Scan how MercadoLibre's earnings setup compares with other heavily reinvesting platforms by reviewing the hand picked 34 high quality undervalued stocks that pair reinvestment with balance sheet strength.

MercadoLibre Investment Narrative Recap

To own MercadoLibre, you need to be comfortable with a business that is trading some profitability today for ecosystem depth in Brazil, especially in logistics and credit. Management is leaning into free shipping, fee cuts and longer duration loans. The key short term catalyst is the November 4 earnings report, where investors will focus on how these choices show up in operating margin and credit metrics.

That 10% share price drop after Brazil's election adds noise but does not change the core question. The biggest risk remains that Brazil focused credit growth and higher leverage combine with any weakening in repayment behavior or legal scrutiny, which could lift funding costs and keep margins under pressure.

The most relevant recent corporate signal is commentary from MercadoLibre's fintech chief that there is no current deceleration or deterioration in Brazil's credit trends despite political shifts and a weaker real. With Brazil providing a little over half of 2025 revenue, that datapoint matters directly to the credit expansion narrative.

Investors watching the November 4 release are effectively testing that statement against fresh data. Asset quality, provisioning and non performing loan ratios will sit alongside logistics efficiency and shipping cost per unit as key proof points. Citi's recent upgrade frames sentiment, but the real driver from here is how consistently MercadoLibre executes on the Brazil credit and logistics playbook.

MercadoLibre's current analyst narrative points to revenues of US$75.8b and earnings of US$5.2b by 2029, based on assumed yearly revenue growth of 29.1% and an increase in earnings of about US$3.3b from US$1.9b today.

Key Takeaways

Nu Holdings stock fell 14% in a month after President Lula unexpectedly won Brazil's Oct. 25 presidential runoff.

MercadoLibre and other US-listed Brazilian stocks fell with it.

Nu's quarterly profit topped $1 billion for the first time in the second quarter.

For investors who can live with Brazil's political swings, the drop looks like a chance to load up.

Nu Holdings (NU:NYSE) stock is down 14% in the past month, and Brazil's voters did most of the damage.

Investors had bet on Flávio Bolsonaro after his surprise first-round showing. Then President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won the Oct. 25 runoff, and Nu sold off along with MercadoLibre (MELI:NASDAQ) and the rest of Brazil's US-listed stocks.

MercadoLibre said its second-quarter revenue grew 50% to $10.2 billion, with Brazil showing the strongest trends. Its report this week covers a quarter that ended before the vote, so what management has seen in Brazil since then matters more than the numbers.

Nu's own news was quieter. On Oct. 23, it said CTO Eric Young is leaving, and CEO David Vélez is overseeing technology until it finds a replacement. Nu says its priorities haven't changed, and its numbers haven't either.

Nu's quarterly profit passed $1 billion

In the second quarter, net income passed $1 billion for the first time, revenue grew 39%, and return on equity hit 33%. On Invest Like the Best on Oct. 13, Vélez said that against the big incumbent banks, "we end up with a return on equity that is 2 to 3x their return on equity."

Investors are pricing Nu as if Lula's win breaks its business, and nothing Nu has reported says it does. With earnings growing and the stock at the bottom of its three-year valuation range, I'd buy, as long as Brazil's swings won't shake you out.

MercadoLibre (NASDAQ:MELI) will report third-quarter earnings on Wednesday at a trying time for the stock.

Shares sold off sharply last week as part of a broader rout in Brazilian stocks after Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won reelection as Brazil's president, contradicting expectations. MercadoLibre is now down 16% year-to-date as profits have fallen due to rising competition and investments in the business.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Will MercadoLibre rise or fall after its earnings report Wednesday afternoon? Let's take a look at what to expect.

Image source: MercadoLibre.

What to expect when MercadoLibre reports

MercadoLibre doesn't provide guidance, which tends to make quarterly reports more volatile, so investors should expect significant movement in the stock after the report, as they have less of a gauge to measure the results.

The analyst consensus calls for revenue to grow 44.6% to $10.7 billion and for earnings per share to increase from $8.32 to $9.27, showing that margins are still expected to narrow.

Investors will be closely watching operating margin as the market is wary of the impact of MercadoLibre's investment cycle. The company is investing in logistics operations after lowering its free shipping threshold in order to remain competitive as entrants like Amazon and Sea Limited's Shopee try to gain market share. Additionally, the company is investing in its credit card business, which has weighed on margins, as the expansion entails upfront marketing and onboarding costs, as well as an accounting adjustment for expected future credit losses, even though no revenue has been collected.

In the third quarter, we're likely to hear something similar about this investment strategy as we did in Q2 when management said its credit book "continues to be very profitable," and added, "It's this overall strength, strong cash generation, robust profitability, and a healthy balance sheet that give us the confidence to keep investing at the pace we are."

Why MercadoLibre stock could jump after the Q3 report

After falling 16% so far this year, there's a good argument that the stock is a bargain. It's recouped some of its losses from the post-election sell-off, but even that decline seemed unreasonable, as the company has done just fine with Lula in charge, putting together an unmatched streak of 30 straight quarters of 30% or better revenue growth.

Can MELI's Cross-Platform Users Unlock Outsized Profit Growth?

AMZN
SE
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

MercadoLibre, Inc. MELI is strengthening its profitability potential by encouraging customers to engage with both its e-commerce marketplace and Mercado Pago fintech services. These customers, referred to as ecosystemic users, represent an increasingly important part of its business model, as deeper participation across both platforms creates opportunities for greater engagement and stronger customer economics.

Ecosystemic users demonstrate significantly higher shopping activity than marketplace-only customers, purchasing more products across a wider range of categories. Their engagement also extends to financial services, where they generate greater payment volumes, maintain higher assets under management and use more financial products. This interconnected activity strengthens the relationship between commerce and fintech, making customers more valuable to the broader ecosystem.

We also note that profit contribution from ecosystemic users substantially exceeds the combined contribution of customers using the marketplace and fintech services separately. This suggests that integrating shopping and financial services creates economic value beyond what either business could generate independently. Mercado Pago credit cards reinforce this relationship by encouraging customers to remain engaged across both platforms.

The growing adoption of cross-platform services underscores MercadoLibre's ability to deepen customer relationships and strengthen monetization opportunities. Management believes this interconnected ecosystem provides a structural competitive advantage that is difficult to replicate.

How Does MercadoLibre Stack Up Against Its Industry?

MercadoLibre, which competes with Amazon.com, Inc. AMZN and Sea Limited SE, has seen its shares tumble 14.4% over the past three months compared with the industry's 15.7% decline. While Amazon shares have fallen 15.4%, Sea Limited has plunged 33.2% in the aforementioned period.

What Does MercadoLibre's Current Valuation Suggest?

From a valuation standpoint, MercadoLibre's forward 12-month price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio is 30.99, higher than the industry average of 18.96. The stock is also trading below its 12-month median level of 34.07. MercadoLibre is trading at a premium to Amazon (forward 12-month P/E of 21.85) and Sea Limited (14.75).

Zacks Investment Research

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

What Do Earnings Estimates Signal for MercadoLibre?

The Zacks Consensus Estimate for MercadoLibre's current fiscal-year sales indicates year-over-year growth of 44.5%, while the consensus estimate for earnings per share suggests a 3.3% decline. For the next fiscal year, the consensus estimates project sales and earnings growth of 29% and 44.9%, respectively.

For the third quarter, the consensus estimates for sales and earnings stand at $10.66 billion and $9.41 per share, suggesting year-over-year growth of 43.8% and 13.1%, respectively.

Zacks Investment Research

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

MELI's Investment Case

MercadoLibre's expanding marketplace presence, strong buyer engagement and integrated commerce-fintech ecosystem support its long-term growth potential. However, persistent margin pressures from strategic investments, softer consumer demand in key markets and a premium valuation remain concerns.

MELI currently carries a Zacks Rank #4 (Sell).

After more than doubling this year, AMD stock is the biggest gainer of the three companies I'm profiling this week. The provider of central processing units (CPUs) and graphics processing units (GPUs) has also more than quadrupled over the past five years.

MercadoLibre Fintech Chief Is "Not Seeing Any Deceleration or Deterioration" in Brazil Credit. November 4 Will Tell ©Yan Krukau from Pexels and Kiattisak Lamchan from kiattisaklamchan via Canva
Key Takeaways

MercadoLibre fell 14% over three months to $1,625, with the steepest drop coming after Lula's surprise runoff win sent Brazilian assets lower on October 26.

Brazil supplied 52.6% of 2025 revenue, so a weaker real and consumer credit now matter more than the 50% sales growth the company posted in the second quarter.

Second-quarter operating margin fell to 6.7% from 12.2% as MercadoLibre cut fees and expanded credit, while Shopee keeps adding capacity in Brazil.

The November 4 report covers a quarter that ended before the election, so management's Brazil commentary matters as much as the numbers.

Brazil voted, and MercadoLibre shareholders paid for it.

MercadoLibre (MELI:NASDAQ) closed Friday at $1,625, down 14% over three months and 32% below its 52-week high of $2,388. The sharpest hit came on October 26, the first trading day after President Lula's surprise runoff win. Shares fell more than 11% early that session as investors dumped Brazilian assets.

Competition isn't easing either. Sea Limited (SE:NYSE) increased capacity for its Shopee marketplace in Brazil by 60% in one year, and it is waiting on regulation to start selling medicine there. That lands right where MercadoLibre is expanding.

MercadoLibre reports third-quarter results on November 4, after the close.

Election night, then the selloff

Three weeks earlier, the mood was very different. Flávio Bolsonaro took 47% of the first-round vote on October 4 against Lula's 45%, and MercadoLibre rallied with Brazilian banks.

The runoff erased that trade. Investors now worry about Brazil's fiscal path, a weaker currency and what both mean for consumer borrowers.

The exposure is hard to overstate:

Brazil generated $15.2 billion of MercadoLibre's $28.9 billion in 2025 revenue.

The company planned to invest about 57 billion reais, roughly $10.9 billion, in Brazil this year, 50% more than in 2025.

It launched one-hour deliveries and expanded its pharmacy business there in September.

The round trip shows up clearly in the share price.

MercadoLibre (MELI): share price, $, May 2026–October 2026 (TIKR)

The stock now trades just 9% above its 52-week low of $1,495.

Growth bought with margin

MercadoLibre's second quarter showed the trade-off it is making. Revenue grew about 50% to more than $10 billion, and GMV rose 36% on an FX-neutral basis. But operating margin fell to 6.7% from 12.2% a year earlier.

That compression is deliberate. The company lowered free-shipping thresholds and seller fees in Brazil, and it kept growing credit fast. Its loan book reached $16.4 billion, up 75%.

Credit quality has held so far. Loans 15 to 90 days past due sat at 7.0%, and credit card NPLs at 4.6%, both near historical lows. "So far, we are not seeing any deceleration or deterioration of credit book in Brazil," fintech president Osvaldo Giménez said on the second-quarter call.

How far has the margin actually fallen?

MercadoLibre (MELI): operating (EBIT) margin (%), quarterly, Q2 2024–Q2 2026 (TIKR)

It roughly halved in a year, so the third quarter needs to show a floor.

Consensus expects third-quarter revenue of about $10.7 billion and EPS of $9.41. The quarter ended September 30, before the runoff, so the reported numbers won't capture the election shock. Fourth-quarter commentary will.

The risks are concrete. A weaker real shrinks Brazil revenue in dollar terms. And if borrowers strain, a loan book that grew 75% in a year could turn from growth engine to drag.

My take: The multiple looks reasonable for a company still growing sales above 40%, and I think the selloff has run ahead of the fundamentals so far. But credit is the swing factor, and the election's impact won't show in the numbers until February. I'd want the November 4 call to sound as calm about Brazil credit as the last one did.

The S&P 500 is hitting new highs, but that doesn't mean every great stock is soaring this year. There are all kinds of reasons a top stock could move down in a strong bull market, and sometimes, that creates investing opportunities.

Consider MercadoLibre (NASDAQ: MELI) and Dutch Bros (NYSE: BROS). Both of these stocks have incredible long-term potential, but they're 37% and 49% off their highs, respectively. Here's why you should buy them on the dip.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

1. MercadoLibre: 37% off highs

MercadoLibre is a Latin American e-commerce superstar. It operates in 18 countries in the region, with a complete platform including logistics, media, and a payments business. Its payments and media businesses have actually become major growth drivers on their own, and the ecosystem puts MercadoLibre in an excellent position to benefit from the shift to digital in Latin America.

It's the largest e-commerce company in its region, and it's building what it expects to be the biggest digital bank in the area as well. It has the most comprehensive logistics program, with 77% of shipments (not chosen to be slow) delivered within 48 hours. Management sees the company's edge in its ecosystem, as artificial intelligence provides consumer recommendations and informs accurate digital ads, and customers on the platform can easily pay through the payments system. That even leads to more users buying insurance policies through the financial platform.

There are 670 million people in Latin America who make up MercadoLibre's addressable market, and the median age is a decade younger than in the U.S. and China. They are also highly connected digitally, even though they lag other regions in e-commerce and digital banking penetration.

MercadoLibre consistently reports high growth, including a 50% increase in revenue year over year in the second quarter, a 56% increase in total payment volume, and a 44% increase in gross merchandise volume.

The stock is down right now because profitability has declined for the past two quarters. Management says it needs to invest to build and grow more, but the market was disappointed.

As soon as profitability starts to increase, the price could go right back up, which is why now is the right time to buy.

Key Takeaways

MercadoLibre stock fell 10% in a week, mostly on Monday, after Lula's surprise win in Brazil's runoff sank Brazilian stocks, Nu Holdings among them.

The worry is currency risk: a weaker real shrinks what MercadoLibre's Brazilian sales are worth in dollars.

Citi upgraded the stock to Buy after the drop, though it trimmed its target.

Third-quarter results on Nov. 4 will show whether operating margin has stopped shrinking.

MercadoLibre (MELI:NASDAQ) stock is down 10% in the past week. Most of the drop came on Monday, the first trading day after President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won Brazil's runoff. Nu Holdings (NU:NYSE) fell 22% before the open that morning.

Nu had more riding on Brazil: almost 118 million of its 139 million customers are there. MercadoLibre is more spread out. Brazil was 52.6% of its 2025 revenue, Mexico 22.4% and Argentina 20.6%. Investors sold it like a Brazil stock anyway.

Investors Bet on the Wrong Candidate

Lula beat Flávio Bolsonaro 51.8% to 48.2% on Oct. 25, weeks after losing the first round. Investors had bet on a market-friendly Bolsonaro win.

Nothing in MercadoLibre's business changed over the weekend. The worry is the real: a weaker one shrinks what its Brazilian sales are worth in dollars. Last quarter the real worked the other way, and Brazil's revenue grew 59% in dollars against 42% FX-neutral.

Wall Street Bought the Dip

On Tuesday, Citi upgraded MercadoLibre to Buy from Neutral, calling the selloff an entry point, though it trimmed its target to $2,050 from $2,100.

Analysts expect normalized EPS to dip to $38.26 this year, then climb to $55.89 in 2027 and $78.56 in 2028:

MELI Normalized EPS Estimates: 2024-2029 (TIKR)

The election reaches those figures mainly through the real: a weaker one trims them in dollars.

MercadoLibre's Nov. 4 Report Is About Margins

MercadoLibre reports third-quarter results on Nov. 4. In the second quarter, revenue rose 50% to $10.2 billion, but operating margin fell to 6.7% from 12.2% a year earlier. The company spent on free shipping, credit and cheaper selling fees while Shopee pushed hard in Brazil.

The quarter ended Sept. 30, before the vote, so watch two things: whether the margin holds near 6.7%, and what management says about Brazil in the fourth quarter, the first with a weaker real.

Tech Stocks Are Selling Off. Here's Why I'd Rather Own MercadoLibre Than Any "Magnificent Seven" Stock.
Will Healy, The Motley Fool

MELI

As anyone who follows the market closely knows, tech stocks have sold off in recent weeks. While the industry delivered on technical breakthroughs and massive revenue growth for investors, rising interest rates, along with concerns about the staggering cost of artificial intelligence (AI) build-outs, weighed on those stocks.

Fortunately, investors have more options than tech and the "Magnificent Seven." In my view, the sell-off is an excellent opportunity to consider other investments. Right now, I hold and periodically add to my position in MercadoLibre (NASDAQ: MELI), and here's why.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
Why MercadoLibre?

Indeed, one might question the choice of MercadoLibre on the surface since it is tech-adjacent. Its e-commerce and fintech platforms depend on technology, and the company has applied AI in many of its applications. Also, in one sense, it can represent a second chance for investors who missed out on Amazon, as MercadoLibre leads the e-commerce market in Latin America.

However, MercadoLibre differs from Amazon in that it is not a cloud service provider. Thus, it has not had the massive capital expenditures (capex) that have weighed on Amazon. In the first half of 2026, MercadoLibre's capex was $712 million, a tiny fraction of the $98 billion Amazon allocated over the same period.

Furthermore, while MercadoLibre has not followed Amazon into the cloud, the consumer discretionary stock has clearly evolved into a conglomerate. Addressing the economic and political challenges in Latin America appears to have inspired that move.

When Latin America was more of a cash-based society and millions could not buy online, Mercado Pago was founded to offer digital financial products to these customers. Mercado Pago went on to serve customers not buying on MercadoLibre's e-commerce site and became the top fintech company in Latin America.

MercadoLibre employed the same strategy to improve logistics. Consequently, that enterprise, Mercado Envios, brought same-day and next-day delivery to the region.

Addressing company struggles

Nonetheless, even for those who can buy into its strategy of turning adversity into opportunity, choosing MercadoLibre may sound counterintuitive. Investors have sold the stock off over the last year. The company cut margins to stave off e-commerce competition and dramatically increased the allowance for doubtful accounts (i.e., bad loans) as it aggressively expands its loan book.

Still, the margin cuts and loan book expansion are likely to dramatically increase revenues and, by extension, profits over time. Also, its past successes should suggest that Brazil's election results are unlikely to derail the company's value proposition.

Additionally, the stock plunged following the surprise reelection of Luiz Inácio Lula Da Silva, as many shareholders perceived his opponent, Flavio Bolsonaro, would have pursued a monetary policy more favorable to MercadoLibre.

Indeed, Brazil is highly critical to the company, as it accounts for about 54% of the company's revenue in the latest quarter. However, investors should recall that MercadoLibre built much of its success by turning Latin America's economic and political challenges into business opportunities, increasing the likelihood it will do so again amid the election turmoil.

MercadoLibre's financials

The company's financials highlight both the opportunity and the adversity.

In the first half of 2026, revenue of $19 billion rose by 49% from year-ago levels. Despite that increase, net income actually fell by 13% over the same period to $883 million. The aforementioned margin cuts and bad-loan expenses weighed on its profits.

Third-quarter earnings also come out on Nov. 4. Analysts are looking for a 45% yearly revenue increase, and although that could imply a slight slowdown, the company is likely to continue growing rapidly.

Also, with the pullback, MercadoLibre trades at a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 45. While that may sound high compared to the S&P 500's average earnings multiple of 26, investors should remember that the company's investments in itself have reduced profits, suggesting the stock is not as overvalued as it appears.

Moreover, MercadoLibre's market cap of $85 billion is a small fraction of Amazon's at $2.7 trillion. That implies MercadoLibre may outperform the Magnificent Seven stocks, whose larger sizes usually make higher-percentage growth more difficult. That advantage suggests it might make sense to buy the dip in MercadoLibre.

Buy MercadoLibre stock

Ultimately, MercadoLibre seems to have Amazon-like growth potential and the smaller size that should help it outperform the Magnificent Seven stocks.

Latin America's challenges, most recently highlighted by Brazil's election, add to the stock's risks. Also, MercadoLibre has had to reduce profits to solidify its e-commerce and fintech business.

Nonetheless, MercadoLibre has thrived by turning adversity into opportunity and should continue to do so. Furthermore, its moves to build market share should increase profits in the long term. Thanks to its smaller size, the stock appears to be gearing up for further growth that could easily reward investors with market-beating returns.
